kernelIdea: p ⇔ q means both p ⇒ q and q ⇒ p. Proving it means writing two proofs.

kernels.l1: Sometimes one sentence is really two promises. You have to keep them both.
kernels.l2: An "exactly when" telling is two promises hiding in one sentence. To show it is kept, check both boxes — one promise each way.
kernels.l3: "A if and only if B" means both if–then claims at once: if A then B, and if B then A. To prove it you must check both boxes, writing one proof for each direction.
kernels.l4: "p if and only if q" is two claims in one: p forces q, and q forces p. Proving it means writing two proofs, and either may be done by contrapositive.
kernels.l5: An if-and-only-if statement asserts that two statements are true in exactly the same cases. Establishing it requires proving both directions separately.
kernels.l6: An if-and-only-if statement holds exactly when both statements have identical truth values. Proof requires both directions, and definitions are almost always if-and-only-if statements in disguise.
kernels.l7: An if-and-only-if statement is two conditionals at once. Proving it means supplying two independent proofs, and each direction may need a different technique.
kernels.l8: p ⇔ q asserts logical equivalence inside the object language; iff-chains are legitimate only when every link is genuinely reversible, and definitions are stipulative if-and-only-if statements.
